newsitem.title: USA: American Air returns to skies after Clinton rescue.
newsitem.headline: American Air returns to skies after Clinton rescue.

text.p: American Airlines, rescued from a devastating pilots' strike by President Bill Clinton, slashed fares on Saturday in a move to woo customers back as thousands of relieved passengers recovered their winter vacations.

The No. 2 U.S. air carrier had almost all of its domestic flights running again on Saturday and was enticing wary travelers with a half-price sale on U.S. and international journeys. Many customers who had feared they would be left stranded at airports were delighted, some whooping with joy as they boarded planes to start their vacations.
"This is great. I was sure we were going to lose out but, hey, here we are, on our way to Honolulu," passenger Jack Moran said at American's home Dallas-Fort Worth airport. "Life is good again."

In Chicago, Amy Rintels packed her bridesmaid's gown and rushed to O'Hare airport when she heard the strike had been averted and she would be able to attend her college roommate's wedding in San Francisco.
"She would have killed me if I couldn't make it," 26-year-old Rintels said. "I couldn't afford to double-book so I just told her I'd do my best to get there."

American officials said system-wide their domestic flights were running at about 58 percent full, down about 10 points from where it would usually be over the long Presidents Day U.S. holiday weekend but still way above expectations.

They said the new discounts of 50 percent and more on domestic and international flights with no advance purchase requirements, and the doubling of frequent flier mile credits, brought a wave of new sales for the weeks ahead. Its reservations switchboards were jammed for much of Saturday.

American carries 20 percent of U.S. air travelers and a grounding of its 2,200 daily flights had been expected to cause havoc in the Caribbean, which is in its peak winter holiday season, and in U.S. cities where American is strong.

Union leaders ordered all 9,300 American pilots to walk off the job at midnight but Clinton stepped in within minutes, using emergency powers to appoint a presidential board that will study the labor dispute and draw up a proposed solution.

The move forced the pilots back to work just 24 minutes into their strike and postponed any new walkout for 60 days. A strike would have cost the airline upwards of $30 million a day and the U.S. economy $100-200 million a day.

Clinton's intervention saved tens of thousands of jobs, at least temporarily, and eliminated fears of traffic chaos but some passengers said the dispute had already wrecked their plans and there were glitches in American's efforts to kickstart its operation.

Dozens of international flights into the United States were canceled on Saturday because American had not allowed the planes to leave U.S. soil on Friday, fearing they would be stranded abroad in the event of a strike.

Sitting with her luggage at Miami airport after an early morning flight from Caracas, Bonnie Margerum said she and her hsuband had been on a week-long fishing trip in the Amazonian jungle and were forced to fly home on a Venezuelan airline because the American flight was canceled. She said changing the tickets had cost them hundreds of dollars but "We just wanted to be back. We had been in the jungle for a while."

Union leaders said they were not pleased by Clinton's intervention and warned the dispute was still far from over. Other American workers, however, were delighted. Skycaps and others hugged each other and slapped co-workers' backs as they arrived for morning shifts at Miami International Airport.

Nearly 80,000 employees at American and its commuter carrier American Eagle would have been placed on unpaid emergency leave if the airline had been shut down. Scores of other businesses ranging from Caribbean hotels to airport gift stores would also have suffered heavy losses.

"This is a wonderful reprieve for everyone," said Marty Heires of Dallas-based LSG/Sky Chefs Inc, the main catering firm for American. The company had expected to lay off at 4,000 employees if American went on strike.

Airline president Don Carty said the loss from the run-up to the strike was already about $100 million. Anxious to halt the loss of passengers to rivals, American announced its sales promotion minutes after Clinton forced pilots back to work.
